title: IISc Honours Maruthi Akella, the Alumnus Whose Algorithms Helped Guide a Lander to the Moon, as Minor Planet Is Named 'Maruthiakella' in His Honour

 News › Learning News › IISc Honours Maruthi Akella, the Alumnus Whose Algorithms Helped Guide a Lander to the Moon, as Mino… IISc Honours Maruthi Akella, the Alumnus Whose Algorithms Helped Guide a Lander to the Moon, as Minor Planet Is Named 'Maruthiakella' in His Honour
 Jasleen Taneja Updated: Nov 12, 2026, 16:27 IST IISc honours Maruthi Akella, whose work helped guide a lander to the Moon; Minor planet named after him Maruthi R Akella is a scientist who studied at IISc’s Department of Aerospace Engineering and completed his ME in 1994. He now holds the Cockrell Family Chair in Engineering at The University of Texas at Austin.
 His research covers how spacecraft work out their position and direction, control systems that adjust themselves, robots that use cameras to see, and the motion of objects in orbit. He is also the Founding Director of the Centre for Autonomous Air Mobility at UT Austin and Editor-in-Chief of The Journal of the ' Astronautical Sciences'. He is currently a VAIBHAV Fellow hosted by IISc.
 How did Maruthi's work reach the Moon ?
 Akella developed algorithms, which are step-by-step instructions for computers, that helped guide Intuitive Machines’ IM-1 lunar lander. 
 In simple terms, the software helped the spacecraft know where it was and steer itself while travelling. The IM-1 mission achieved the first US Moon landing in more than 50 years.
 In recognition of his contributions, minor planet 5376 has been named 'Maruthiakella'.
 The five Distinguished Alumni of 2026
 These awards recognise alumni who have made exceptional contributions to their professions, society and the Institute.
 Awardee Role Known for 
 Maruthi R Akella Professor, UT Austin Spacecraft guidance and control, including IM-1 
 B S Manjunath Computer scientist, UC Santa Barbara Computer vision and image software 
 Dipankar Das Sarma Physicist, ANRF National Science Chair Materials and condensed matter physics 
 Jagannath Nayak Director General, Missiles and Strategic Systems, DRDO Defence navigation technology 
 Rajat Moona Director, IIT Gandhinagar India’s digital infrastructure 
 What did the other winners achieve?
 B S Manjunath works on computer vision, which helps computers understand images, and on scientific image informatics. 
 He helped develop BisQue, an open-source platform that became a core service of the US National Science Foundation’s CyVerse. He also contributed video descriptors to the MPEG-7 standard, which is used to describe video content.
 Dipankar Das Sarma has advanced the understanding of materials and condensed matter physics, which studies how solids and liquids behave. He also helped secure India’s access to international synchrotron facilities, which are powerful research tools, by setting up the Indo-Italian beamlines at Elettra.
 Jagannath Nayak led the indigenous development of high-accuracy Fibre Optic Gyroscopes, which are sensors that track direction, for defence programmes such as Akash, Nag and Astra. He also contributed to India’s first operational Laser Directed Energy Weapon system.
 Rajat Moona has helped shape India’s digital infrastructure. His work includes the technology behind driving licences, e-passports, electronic voting machines, VVPAT and the Electronic Toll Collection system, including FASTag. 
 He also contributed to India’s supercomputing capabilities as Director General of C-DAC.
 Three young researchers also honoured
 IISc will also give its Young Alumnus/Alumna Medals to three researchers under 40. These are:
 Abhishek Sinha , Reader at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, Mumbai, works in theoretical computer science, especially online learning and network optimisation.
 Geethu Joseph , tenured Assistant Professor at Delft University of Technology, Netherlands, works on sparse control, intelligent sensing and autonomous systems.
 Himanshu Joshi , Assistant Professor of Biotechnology at IIT Hyderabad, specialises in computational biophysics, molecular simulations and DNA nanotechnology, including artificial water channels and DNA-based ion channels.
 When will the awards be presented?
 The awardees will be felicitated on December 19, 2026 , at the JN Tata Auditorium on the IISc campus.
 IISc Director Prof G Rangarajan said it is wonderful to see alumni make a mark in different fields and contribute to society. He said the awards celebrate their journeys and recognise the many ways they continue to inspire the IISc community. 
 Nominations are evaluated by a committee under the Director’s oversight.
 These eight scientists work in very different areas, from space and defence to digital services and biology. The list shows how graduates of one institute are shaping technology in India and abroad. For students, it is also a reminder that careers in science can reach as far as the Moon.
